facts.text: A job description is a marketing document, a legal document, and a filter - at the same time. It must attract candidates the company wants, deter candidates who would be a poor fit, comply with US pay-transparency law in 15+ states, and avoid language that systematically suppresses applications from underrepresented groups.

facets.title: 1. The structural skeleton: what you'll do / what we look for / what we offer

facts.text: What you'll do - Responsibilities. Day-to-day work. Outcomes the role owns.
What we look for - Requirements split into must-haves (3-5 dealbreakers) and nice-to-haves.
What we offer - Compensation range, benefits, growth path, working model.

facets.title: 2. Responsibilities vs requirements: keep them separated

facts.text: Responsibilities describe what the person does. Verbs in the present tense: "Design and ship," "Mentor," "Own."
Requirements describe what the person must already have. Adjectives and nouns: "5 years of," "Experience with," "Familiarity with."

facets.title: 3. Must-haves vs nice-to-haves — and the application-gap evidence

facts.text: Cap must-haves at 3-5. A must-have is a dealbreaker - if the candidate doesn't have it, you won't hire them.

The evidence: Women apply for jobs only when they meet ~56% of listed requirements vs men at ~52%. Long requirement lists deter applications from underrepresented groups more than from majority groups (Bohnet 2016).
Heuristic: If your must-haves list has more than 5 items, ask which two you'd drop. Then drop them.

facets.title: 4. Inclusive language: the gender-coded word audit

facts.text: Textio's research found that gender-coded language measurably skews who applies.

Masculine-coded words to avoid: aggressive, ambitious, analytical, assertive, challenge, competitive, confident, decisive, determined, dominant, driven, fearless, forceful, independent, ninja, outspoken, principled, rockstar, self-reliant, superior.
Action: Run the JD through a tool like Textio, Gender Decoder, or Datapeople. Aim for balance or feminine-leaning if the role is historically male-coded.
States requiring salary range disclosure (verify before posting):
California (15+ employees) - required
Colorado (all employers with 1+ CO employee) - required
Illinois (15+ employees, effective Jan 2025) - required
Massachusetts (25+ employees, effective Oct 2025) - required
New York - required statewide
Washington (15+ employees) - required + benefits description
Practical rule: If you post a JD that may be viewed from any of these jurisdictions, include a good-faith salary range.
Age bias signals: "digital native," "energetic," "fast-paced young team."
Education bias: "degree from a top university" - replace with the actual skill.
Cultural-fit signals: "must love startups," "we're a family." These select for sameness.
Rockstar / ninja / guru / wizard / superstar / 10x. Gender-coded and exclusionary.
The 20-item must-haves list. Cap at 3-5.
"Competitive salary." Non-compliant in 15+ states.
"Digital native" / "energetic" / "fast-paced young team." Age-coded.
Years-of-experience inflation. "10+ years of React" - React is 13 years old.
[ ] Salary range posted if applicants in CA, CO, HI, IL, ME, MD, MA, MN, NJ, NY, VT, WA, or DC may apply.
[ ] Benefits summary included (required in CO, WA).
[ ] Equal-opportunity statement included.
[ ] Reasonable-accommodation contact provided.
